'''''Saccharum spontaneum''''' ('''wild sugarcane''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SASP|taxon=Saccharum spontaneum|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> '''kans grass''') is a [[poaceae|grass]] native throughout much of [[tropical]] and [[subtropical]] [[Asia]], northern [[Australia]], and eastern and northern [[Africa]].<ref name="powo">{{cite web |title=Saccharum spontaneum L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:420031-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew |access-date=14 January 2024}}</ref> It is a perennial grass, growing up to three meters in height, with spreading [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] roots.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://assamforest.in/publication/wildEdible_plantsAssam.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203013608/http://www.assamforest.in/publication/wildEdible_plantsAssam.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://assamplants.com/Alphabetical%20%20Order%20(Sc%20Name).htm |title=www.assamplants.com { A database of medicinal plants of Assam for a green future } |website=assamplants.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110507015653/http://assamplants.com/Alphabetical%20%20Order%20(Sc%20Name).htm |archive-date=2011-05-07}}</ref>

The plant has hybridized with ''[[Saccharum officinarum]]'', a domesticated [[sugarcane]]. The hybridization has produced ''[[Saccharum barberi]]'' and ''[[Saccharum sinense]]''.<ref name="Paterson2012">{{cite book|first1=Andrew H. |last1=Paterson|first2=Paul H.|last2=Moore|first3=Tew|last3=Tom L.|editor1-first=Andrew H. |editor1-last=Paterson|title =Genomics of the Saccharinae|chapter =The Gene Pool of ''Saccharum'' Species and Their Improvement|publisher =Springer Science & Business Media|year =2012|pages=43–72|isbn = 9781441959478|chapter-url =https://books.google.com/books?id=F282fp_IMI8C&pg=PA54}}</ref>
<!--THE FOLLOWING NEEDS A REWRITEN FOR A GLOBAL VIEWPOINT AND SOURCED
Commonly found in the [[Terai-Duar savanna and grasslands]], a lowland [[ecoregion]] at the base of the [[Himalaya]] range in [[Pakistan]], [[Nepal]], [[India]], [[Bangladesh]] and [[Bhutan]]. Kans grass colonises exposed silt plains created each year by the retreating [[monsoon]] floods, forming almost pure stands on the lowest portions of the floodplain. Kans [[grassland]]s are an important habitat for the [[Indian rhinoceros]] (''Rhinoceros unicornis''). In Nepal, kans grass is harvested to thatch roofs or fence vegetable gardens.

The ability to quickly colonize disturbed soil has allowed it to become an [[invasive species]] that takes over croplands and pasturelands, as has been documented in the Republic of Panama.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Saltonstall|first1=Kristin|last2=Bonnett|first2=Graham D.|last3=Aitken|first3=Karen S.|date=2020-11-21|title=A perfect storm: ploidy and preadaptation facilitate Saccharum spontaneum escape and invasion in the Republic of Panama|journal=Biological Invasions|volume=23|issue=4|pages=1101–1115|language=en|doi=10.1007/s10530-020-02421-3|issn=1573-1464|doi-access=free}}</ref>

''Saccharum spontaneum'' has a considerable number of regional names in the Indian Subcontinent, ''kash'' (কাশ) being common in [[Bengali language|Bengali]], ''kohuwa'' (কঁহুৱা) in [[Assamese language|Assamese]], ''kasatandi'' (କାଶତଣ୍ଡୀ) in [[Odia language|Odia]] and ''Kasi'' (खासि) in [[Boro language (India)|Bodo]].  The use of  Saccharum spontaneum is also found in [[Ayurveda]].<ref>[http://www.botanical.com/site/column_poudhia/116_janjgir.html Pankaj Oudhia (2001-3)]</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://assamplants.com/All%20Species/Saccharum%20spont.htm |title=Assam Plants |website=assamplants.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131207013229/http://assamplants.com/All%20Species/Saccharum%20spont.htm |archive-date=2013-12-07}}</ref>

A set of species-related orphane genes, ''Saccharum spontaneum'' exhibits exceptional resistance to [[biotic stress]]es such as [[nematode]]s, [[fungus|fungi]], [[bacterium|bacteria]] and other pests and diseases, and [[abiotic stress]]es such as cold, drought, salinity and nutritionally [[soil fertility|deficient soil]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.3389/fpls.2022.923069 |doi-access=free |title=Taxonomically Restricted Genes Are Associated with Responses to Biotic and Abiotic Stresses in Sugarcane (Saccharum SPP.) |year=2022 |last1=Cardoso-Silva |first1=Cláudio Benício |last2=Aono |first2=Alexandre Hild |last3=Mancini |first3=Melina Cristina |last4=Sforça |first4=Danilo Augusto |last5=Da Silva |first5=Carla Cristina |last6=Pinto |first6=Luciana Rossini |last7=Adams |first7=Keith L. |last8=De Souza |first8=Anete Pereira |journal=Frontiers in Plant Science |volume=13 |pmc=9280035 }}</ref>-->
